problem: Existing social navigation simulators either give no visual observations (2D), have no moving humans (static 3D), or use mesh rendering, random or hand-crafted pedestrian goals and looping mocap gaits. This leaves a visual and behavioral gap and limits vision-based social navigation research.
motivation: Social navigation is moving toward end-to-end policies that use only onboard visual observations. Such policies need photorealistic scenes, natural pedestrian appearance and motion, and semantically plausible behavior, and real-world data is too costly to collect at scale. A faithful simulator and benchmark are needed to diagnose current methods and to supply transferable training data.
key_idea: Represent both scenes and human avatars with 3D Gaussian splatting, drive pedestrians with LLM-generated semantic intents, plan their paths with a crowd planner, and animate them with a trajectory-conditioned motion generator, then build a difficulty-stratified benchmark (SONG-Bench) with multi-dimensional metrics.
insight: Zero-shot baselines nearly all fail (SR below 22% on Easy, near 0 on Hard). Failures are dominated by obstacle and human collisions, and high failure persists even in avatar-free scenes (SR 23-41%), so basic geometric safety and collision recovery precede social etiquette. NoMaD, trained on real-world data, handles dynamic humans best, yet the gap among methods largely vanishes in avatar-free scenes, which suggests that handling dynamic humans is the discriminative bottleneck and that data realism matters more than model scale. Fine-tuning NavDP on replayed data from the platform doubles real-world success, though absolute numbers stay low.
method: Gaussian asset library: 1,000 SAGE-3D 3DGS scenes with a geometry proxy and top-down semantic/traversability map; 500 animatable Gaussian avatars (195 HumanGS-style avatars from DNA-Rendering, about 6 h each, and 305 LHM reconstructions from GPT-Image2 images, about 2 min each).
Semantic intent generation: Gemini 3.1 Flash reads the semantic map and object labels and outputs (activity, start, goal) intents, which are filtered by traversability and occupancy constraints.

Multi-avatar trajectory planning: a Recast/DetourCrowd planner turns intents into jointly planned root trajectories with pedestrian-pedestrian collision avoidance; crowded or infeasible configurations are replanned or removed.

Motion and avatar binding: Kimodo synthesizes full-body motion from each trajectory (fixed walking text prompt), followed by trajectory alignment, resampling, smoothing and foot-ground correction. Gaussian avatars are then bound to the motions and cached per episode.

Closed-loop runtime: Isaac Lab handles the robot and static collisions, while the Gaussian layer renders RGB-D on demand (10 steps/s in the full loop). Avatar collision is flagged when more than 5 avatar Gaussian centers fall inside a 0.2 m robot collision volume.

SONG-Bench: 500 point-goal episodes from four sampling modes (co-directional, counter-directional, encounter, random). They are graded easy/medium/hard (200/200/100) by path length, turns, avatar encounters and corridor width, and scored on SR, SPL, STL, TO, AvgT, CR_obs, CR_hum, PSC, MinD and JK, with human teleoperation as an upper bound.

Sim-to-real data: about 2k trajectories replayed in the platform, from successful rollouts of a fine-tuned Height planner (with privileged pedestrian and obstacle positions) plus human teleoperation, are used to fine-tune NavDP.

setting.backbone: Benchmarked baselines NoMaD, NavDP, iPlanner and SocialNav (zero-shot, public weights); NavDP fine-tuned for transfer; the platform uses Gemini 3.1 Flash, Kimodo, HumanGS/LHM, and Recast/DetourCrowd
setting.training_data: Benchmark evaluation is zero-shot with public weights. NavDP is fine-tuned on about 2k replayed trajectories from the platform (Height-planner successes plus human teleoperation, the Height planner being trained on 5k episodes over 500 scenarios).
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (960x540 in the standalone renderer, 854x480 in the closed loop) plus relative goal coordinate; camera 0.8 m high, 70° HFOV
setting.action_space: low-level velocity commands (max 0.5 m/s linear, 45°/s angular), 10 Hz, 200-step budget; the policies output trajectories/waypoints that are tracked
setting.simulator: Isaac Lab with a custom 3D Gaussian splatting renderer (SONG)
setting.privileged: none at test time for the benchmarked policies; the Height planner used to generate fine-tuning data had privileged pedestrian and obstacle positions

numbers.backbone: NoMaD (public weights, image-goal rendered at goal)
numbers.extra: Human teleop upper bound on Easy: SR 95.5

numbers_note: SONG-Bench is introduced by this paper and the numbers are for benchmarked baselines rather than a proposed policy. The only own-method numbers are the fine-tuned NavDP real-world results. Full baseline results are in Table main_results (NoMaD, NavDP, iPlanner, SocialNav, human teleop) and the avatar-free ablation table, and only NoMaD rows are listed above.
results: All four zero-shot baselines score at most 21.5% SR on Easy (NoMaD best; NavDP 12.5, iPlanner 15.0, SocialNav 19.0) and 0-3% on Hard, versus 95.5% (Easy) and 80.0% (Hard) for human teleoperation. Fine-tuning NavDP on the platform's data raises real-world SR from 10% to 20% (one pedestrian) and from 5% to 10% (two pedestrians) on a Unitree Go2.
limitations: Avatar collision is approximated by counting Gaussian centers in a robot volume with a fixed threshold, which is not true body-level contact.
Pedestrians follow prescribed trajectories and do not react to the robot, so reciprocal human-robot interaction is not evaluated.

Real-world evidence is small and weak (20 trials per setting, absolute SR only 10-20%), and the 'data realism beats model scale' claim is inferred from confounded baselines with no controlled ablation.
